description: comp sci students, working to build effective software solutions.
summary: Lunar Site Navigator is a web app that shows when a Moon landing site can see the Sun and Earth. Using NASA Horizons and LOLA terrain data, it gives plain-language countdowns, a horizon view and site comparisons, so planners and the public can judge sites and dates at the south pole.
details:
Lunar Site Navigator (LSN)

What it does and how it works

LSN is a web app that shows when a landing site on the Moon can see the Sun and the Earth. Near the Moon’s south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees above the horizon, so a single hill or crater rim can hide it, or the Earth, for days.

The app has three main pages:

  • Sky view gives three numbers in plain words: how high the Sun is, how long until it sets or rises, and how long until the Earth sets or rises. Below that is a picture of the full horizon as seen from the site, with the real hills, the Sun and the Earth, and a Play button to move through time.
  • Compare places puts two to four sites side by side for the same dates and marks which has the most sunlight and the shortest dark periods.
  • Rover sim shows a recording of our simulated rover driving from sunlight into a deep shadow at Connecting Ridge and keeping track of its own position.

The Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons, every 10 minutes for three years. The hills come from NASA’s LOLA height map of the south pole. We process both once into two small files, so the app runs entirely in the browser with no server.

Benefits

NASA’s existing tools for this question are powerful but built for experts. LSN answers it in seconds, in words anyone can read, on a phone or a laptop. It covers eight places near the south pole (close to areas NASA named for Artemis III) and the six Apollo landing sites.

Intended impact

We want mission planners, teachers and the public to see quickly why site and date matter at the lunar south pole: sunlight is needed for power and heat, and a clear view of Earth is needed for direct radio. The app shows where the Sun and Earth are; it does not calculate power or radio quality, and it says so. The rover simulation shows the next step: what a rover can do when a place is dark.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Planner: TypeScript, React, Vite, Node.js, Vitest and ESLint. Hosted on Vercel.
  • Rover simulation: Python, ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic and RViz 2 on Ubuntu 24.04, using laser-scanner and motion-sensor SLAM.
  • Data: NASA JPL Horizons, NASA LOLA elevation models (PGDA), the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature and NASA NSSDC Apollo coordinates.
  • Hardware: laptops only. The rover is simulated; no physical hardware was built.
  • AI: parts of the code and documents were written with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic). All data comes from the NASA and IAU sources above, not from AI.

How it is creative

  • It turns orbital data into a picture people already understand: standing at the site and looking at the horizon.
  • Every number comes with a sentence saying what it means, for example “This place has sunlight for this long. Then the dark starts.”
  • It joins two views of the same place: the planner shows when Connecting Ridge is dark, and the rover simulation shows a rover working in that dark.

Factors we considered

  • Trust: we checked our results against NASA sources. Our Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.006 degrees, and our sunlight share at three sites is within 2 to 6 percentage points of NASA’s published illumination map.
  • Honesty: the app states its limits. Our south-pole places are high points we found on the height map, not official landing sites.
  • Simple words: we replaced expert terms with plain ones so a first-time visitor is not lost.
  • Access: it works at phone width, uses colours that stay distinct for colour-blind users, and needs no account or install.
  • Reproducibility: all data files can be rebuilt from the NASA sources with the scripts in the repository.

Live app: https://lunarsitenavigator-five.vercel.app
Code: https://github.com/umunna/lunar_site_navigator
